name: Ginkgo biloba

card.summary: Leaf extract of the ancient ginkgo tree sold as a memory and circulation supplement; large reviews find no conclusive benefit and it carries bleeding-interaction cautions.
card.note: May interact with anticoagulant and antiplatelet drugs; IARC lists the extract as possibly carcinogenic (Group 2B).

quick.overview:
Ginkgo biloba extract comes from the leaves of the ginkgo tree, a "living fossil" native to China. It has long been used in traditional Chinese medicine and is now one of the best-known herbal supplements for memory and circulation.

Wikipedia reports that no high-quality evidence supports its use for memory or attention in healthy people and that the US NCCIH says it has not been conclusively proven effective for any condition. In the EU a standardised extract is registered as a herbal medicine for mild dementia. It is not an appearance treatment.
quick.mechanism: Extracts contain flavonoids and terpene lactones and have been studied for antioxidant and blood-flow related effects; the mechanisms behind any clinical effect remain unsettled.
quick.risks: Reported effects include stomach upset, headache, dizziness and bleeding risk, and interactions with warfarin and antiplatelet drugs are a concern. Ginkgolic acids can cause allergic skin reactions and eating many raw seeds can cause ginkgotoxin poisoning. IARC classified the extract as a possible carcinogen in 2016.

lead: Ginkgo biloba, the ginkgo or maidenhair tree, is a long-lived deciduous tree native to China and the only living species in its order.[1][2] Standardised leaf extracts, most often the extract known as EGb 761, are sold as supplements and, in some European countries, as herbal medicines.[1][11]

In appearance-focused and lifting communities, ginkgo is taken as a general focus and circulation supplement. The chain people describe runs from sharper concentration and better blood flow to more consistent training and productive days, and, in a few forum posts, to a stronger session in the gym.[12][13][14] Proponents point to mechanisms reviewed in the literature, including increased cerebral blood flow and antioxidant and antiplatelet effects attributed to the extract's flavone and terpene lactone content.[11]

Wikipedia reports use in traditional Chinese medicine since at least the 11th century and states that there is no conclusive evidence for any of its traditional uses.[1] The US NCCIH has said it has never been conclusively proven effective for any condition, while a 2014 European Medicines Agency committee concluded that the leaf extract is effective and safe for improving cognition in mild dementia.[1] Safety topics include bleeding risk with blood thinners and the IARC's 2016 Group 2B classification of the extract.[1]
infobox: Not an approved drug; sold as supplement

paras: Carl Linnaeus described the species in 1771; biloba refers to the twice-lobed leaf. The genus name is traced to Engelbert Kaempfer, who recorded it in Nagasaki in 1690, and is regarded as a mistranscription of the Japanese ginkyo.[1] Fossils related to modern ginkgo date to the early Permian, and the tree is widely called a living fossil. Specimens over 1,600 years old have been measured, and six trees within 1 to 2 km of the 1945 Hiroshima blast survived.[1]

Leaf extracts contain flavonoid glycosides (myricetin, kaempferol, isorhamnetin, quercetin), proanthocyanidins, biflavones and terpene trilactones, namely ginkgolides and bilobalide, together with alkylphenols such as ginkgolic acids that standardised preparations limit.[1] Pharmacokinetic work has compared how well different ginkgo extract forms are absorbed.[16][23]

Seeds, nuts and leaves were used in traditional Chinese medicine for dementia, asthma, bronchitis and kidney and bladder disorders.[1] Modern extracts are marketed for memory, circulation and cognition.[2]

In supplement culture ginkgo is sold alone or in multi-ingredient nootropic and pre-workout blends and multivitamins; a T Nation poster notes it among herbs taken for focus alongside panax ginseng and caffeine, and a 2010 forum thread asks about stacking it with L-tyrosine.[12][17] A lifter in another thread jokes that ginkgo is helping his lockout, and a 2002 post compares vinpocetine's effect to ginkgo as a pre-workout focus aid.[18][19]

Reviews describe proposed mechanisms including increased cerebral blood flow, antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects, and antiplatelet activity linked to the flavone and terpene lactone constituents. Clinical doses in trials have ranged widely, and optimal dose, duration and long-term effects were flagged for future work.[11] A systematic review of plant-derived nootropics found ginkgo the most relevant plant for perceptual and motor functions, while noting inconsistencies across studies.[20]

Wikipedia summarises recent reviews: a 2023 review found insufficient clinical evidence for therapeutic use; systematic reviews found no benefit for hypertension, menopause-related cognitive problems, tinnitus, post-stroke recovery or altitude sickness; a 2016 systematic review found reduced tardive dyskinesia symptoms in people with schizophrenia; a 2021 umbrella review suggested possible benefit in Alzheimer's disease while a 2023 analysis found insufficient evidence; and a 2026 Cochrane review found little to no meaningful benefit for mild cognitive impairment and low-certainty, small to moderate improvements in dementia symptoms.[1]

A large registered prevention trial enrolled 3,069 older adults to examine dementia and Alzheimer's disease.[3] A trial of ginkgo in mild-to-moderate dementia was also used to measure the Hawthorne effect, comparing minimal and intensive follow-up.[4] Other registered studies have looked at Raynaud's phenomenon[5], glaucoma[6], schizophrenia[7], mild cognitive impairment with cerebrovascular disease[8] and cerebral insufficiency[9]; registry entries describe design, not outcomes.

The Ginkgo Evaluation of Memory prevention trial (NCT00010803) enrolled 3,069 older adults from 2000 and was published in JAMA in 2008 to determine whether ginkgo versus placebo lowered incidence of all-cause dementia and Alzheimer disease in people with normal cognition or mild cognitive impairment, which the authors noted had lacked adequately powered trials.[3][21] A 2023 systematic review of plant nootropics found ginkgo the most relevant nootropic for perceptual and motor domains.[20] A small open-label 2025 study examined a polyherbal medicine for cognition in healthy older adults.[22]

Wikipedia lists bleeding risk, gastrointestinal upset, headache, dizziness, palpitations and restlessness. Ginkgolic acids and related alkylphenols can cause allergic skin reactions, particularly in people allergic to poison ivy, mango or cashew; large seed intake over time can cause ginkgotoxin poisoning with convulsions.[1] Supplements may affect anticoagulant and antiplatelet drug therapy.[1] A general review of herb-drug interactions also discusses ginkgo among other herbs.[10]

The International Agency for Research on Cancer classified ginkgo extract as possibly carcinogenic to humans (Group 2B) in 2016. In 2014 the EMA herbal committee reached the conclusion above for mild dementia. In the United States it is not an approved drug, and the FDA issued warning letters in 2021 to 2023 over false health claims.[1]

lore.intro: Ginkgo appears in T Nation supplement threads as a focus and circulation herb, often grouped with other nootropics.[12][17]

claims.claim: Ginkgo boosts focus and memory in healthy people.
claims.believers: Forum users list it among brain-function supplements and say it helps with focus and ADD symptoms alongside ginseng and caffeine.[12][14][17]
claims.experts: A 2008 JAMA trial tested dementia incidence in older adults, and Wikipedia summarises reviews with insufficient evidence for therapeutic use, while the EMA endorsed the extract for mild dementia cognition.[21][1]

claims.claim: Ginkgo improves blood flow so training performs better.
claims.believers: A lifter jokes that his heaviest lockout came while taking ginkgo, and others group it with vinpocetine as a pre-workout focus aid.[18][19]
claims.experts: Reviews attribute increased cerebral blood flow to the extract, while the NCCIH says it has not been conclusively proven effective for any condition.[11][1]

claims.claim: Ginkgo is safe because it is natural.
claims.believers: Supplement users treat it as a gentle herb.[12]
claims.experts: Wikipedia lists bleeding risk, interactions with anticoagulants, allergy to ginkgolic acids and IARC Group 2B classification of the extract.[1]
